subject: Biology
description: Human liver — anatomy, functions (detoxification, bile, glucose storage), associated diseases (hepatitis, cirrhosis), gallbladder, hepatic portal system.

questions.stem: The LIVER is the LARGEST internal organ. Its weight in an average adult is approximately:
questions.explanation: LIVER — largest internal organ; weight ~1.4-1.6 kg in adult human. Largest GLAND too. LOCATION: upper-right abdomen, below diaphragm; mostly hidden behind ribcage. STRUCTURE: 4 lobes (right, left, caudate, quadrate); ~80% is hepatocytes (functional cells); ~20% is structural + blood vessels. UNIQUE BLOOD SUPPLY: gets ~75% blood from PORTAL VEIN (carrying nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from intestines, stomach, spleen) + 25% from HEPATIC ARTERY (oxygenated blood). 'Hepatic Portal System' — blood passes through liver BEFORE returning to heart, allowing detoxification + nutrient processing. KEY FUNCTIONS (~500 known): (1) DETOXIFICATION (alcohol, drugs, ammonia → urea). (2) METABOLISM — converts excess glucose to glycogen for storage. (3) PROTEIN SYNTHESIS — albumin, clotting factors, bile. (4) BILE production (~1 L/day) — emulsifies fats; stored in gallbladder. (5) STORAGE — vitamins (A, D, E, K, B12), iron, copper. (6) IMMUNE — Kupffer cells (resident macrophages). (7) HORMONE breakdown. REGENERATIVE POWER: liver is one of the few organs that can REGROW from as little as 25% of original mass (used in living-donor liver transplants). RELATED MYTH: PROMETHEUS (Greek mythology) — Zeus condemned him to have his liver eaten daily by an eagle, regrowing each night. PYQ FREQUENCY: liver basics in NEET, NCERT Class 11 — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: BILE, secreted by the liver, is stored in the:
questions.explanation: BILE — yellow-green fluid produced by hepatocytes (~1 L/day). Stored in the GALLBLADDER (under right lobe of liver), and RELEASED into the small intestine via the BILE DUCT during fat-rich meals. FUNCTION: bile EMULSIFIES large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing surface area for lipase (enzyme) action — enables fat digestion. COMPONENTS: (1) BILE SALTS (cholic acid, glycocholic acid) — emulsifying agents. (2) BILE PIGMENTS — BILIRUBIN (yellow-orange, from RBC breakdown) and BILIVERDIN (green). (3) Cholesterol, lecithin, water, electrolytes. JAUNDICE — yellow skin/eye coloration when BILIRUBIN accumulates (failure of liver, blocked bile duct, or excess RBC breakdown). CAUSES: hepatitis, gallstones, bile duct cancer, hemolytic anemia. GALLSTONES: cholesterol stones (most common in West, India), pigment stones (Asians + sickle cell anemia). FEMALE > male incidence; risks: obesity, rapid weight loss, pregnancy, certain medications. CHOLECYSTECTOMY (gallbladder removal) — common surgery (~5 lakh/year in India). After removal, bile drips continuously into intestine — most people adapt; some get fat-malabsorption. INTERESTING: in many traditional medical systems (Ayurveda, TCM) — yellow bile / pitta = passion, anger; black bile / melancholy. PYQ FREQUENCY: bile-gallbladder in NEET, NCERT Class 11 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: The liver stores excess glucose as:
questions.explanation: GLYCOGEN — branched polymer of glucose; the BODY's MAIN STORAGE FORM of carbohydrate. Stored in LIVER (~100 g, ~5% of liver weight) and SKELETAL MUSCLE (~400 g, ~1% of muscle weight). PROCESS: when blood glucose is HIGH (after meals), insulin signals liver/muscle to convert glucose → glycogen (GLYCOGENESIS). When blood glucose drops (between meals, exercise), GLUCAGON signals liver to break down glycogen → glucose (GLYCOGENOLYSIS). KEY DIFFERENCE: LIVER glycogen → released as glucose into bloodstream for whole body. MUSCLE glycogen → used LOCALLY by muscle (no enzyme to release glucose to blood). ENERGY VALUE: total body glycogen ~2,000 kcal — enough for ~1 day of basic energy; depleted in prolonged fasting/strenuous exercise (marathon runners 'hit the wall' when glycogen runs out at ~20 miles). DIABETES MELLITUS: type 1 (insulin deficiency) or type 2 (insulin resistance) — disrupts this glucose-glycogen balance; blood glucose stays high, leading to vascular damage. ASSOCIATED HORMONES: INSULIN (from pancreas beta cells) — lowers blood glucose. GLUCAGON (alpha cells) — raises it. GROWTH HORMONE, CORTISOL — also regulate. PARALLEL: PLANTS store excess glucose as STARCH (similar polymer); CELLULOSE is for cell walls (different bonding). PYQ FREQUENCY: glycogen-liver in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: HEPATITIS is inflammation of which organ?
questions.explanation: HEPATITIS — inflammation of the LIVER. Etymology: 'hepar/hepatos' (Greek for liver) + '-itis' (inflammation). VIRAL HEPATITIS — 5 main types: (1) HEP A — fecal-oral; acute, usually self-limiting; vaccine available. (2) HEP B — blood/sexual; can be CHRONIC, leading to cirrhosis/cancer; vaccine available (universal newborn vaccination). (3) HEP C — blood (esp. shared needles, transfusions before screening); high chronic risk; CURED by direct-acting antivirals (DAA, since 2014, ~95% cure). NO vaccine for HCV. (4) HEP D — coinfection with HEP B. (5) HEP E — fecal-oral; common in India (often transmitted via contaminated water); particularly dangerous in pregnant women. NON-VIRAL HEPATITIS: alcohol, autoimmune, drugs (acetaminophen overdose), fatty liver disease (NAFLD). INDIA STATS: ~4 crore HBV chronic carriers; ~1 crore HCV; HEP E common during monsoon flooding. WORLD HEPATITIS DAY: 28 July (Dr. Baruch Blumberg's birthday — Nobel 1976 for HBV discovery). SUFFIX '-itis' = inflammation. EXAMPLES: NEPHRITIS (kidney), GASTRITIS (stomach), ARTHRITIS (joints), DERMATITIS (skin), MENINGITIS (meninges), TONSILLITIS, BRONCHITIS, ENCEPHALITIS (brain). PYQ FREQUENCY: hepatitis in NEET, AIIMS, SSC GA — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: CIRRHOSIS is a condition where the liver:

options.option_text: Has cells that multiply too quickly

questions.explanation: CIRRHOSIS — chronic, irreversible LIVER FIBROSIS / SCARRING. Healthy liver tissue gets replaced by SCAR TISSUE; impairs blood flow + function. CAUSES (in order of frequency in INDIA): (1) ALCOHOL ABUSE — alcoholic liver disease; major cause globally. (2) HEPATITIS B/C — chronic infection. (3) NAFLD/NASH (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/Steatohepatitis) — rising rapidly with obesity, metabolic syndrome; major emerging cause. (4) AUTOIMMUNE hepatitis. (5) GENETIC — hemochromatosis (iron overload), Wilson's disease (copper), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. STAGES: simple fatty liver → steatohepatitis → fibrosis → cirrhosis → liver failure / hepatocellular carcinoma (cancer). SYMPTOMS in advanced cirrhosis: fatigue, jaundice, ascites (fluid in abdomen), spider angiomata (spider-web blood vessels on skin), confusion (hepatic encephalopathy from ammonia accumulation), bleeding tendencies (poor clotting factor synthesis), portal hypertension → esophageal varices (deadly bleeding). DIAGNOSIS: blood tests (LFT — liver function tests), ultrasound, FibroScan, biopsy. TREATMENT: stop the cause + manage complications; severe cases need LIVER TRANSPLANT. INDIA — major issue: ~25% of urban Indians have NAFLD. PYQ FREQUENCY: cirrhosis in NEET, AIIMS PG entrance.

questions.stem: Which protein, synthesized by liver, is the MOST ABUNDANT in human blood plasma?
questions.explanation: ALBUMIN — most abundant plasma protein (~3.5-5 g/dL; ~60% of total plasma proteins). Synthesized BY THE LIVER (~12-15 g/day). FUNCTIONS: (1) MAINTAINS COLLOID OSMOTIC PRESSURE (oncotic pressure) — keeps fluid in blood vessels (prevents edema). (2) TRANSPORTS — bilirubin, fatty acids, calcium, hormones (thyroid, cortisol), drugs (warfarin, penicillin). (3) Buffer — minor pH-buffering role. PLASMA PROTEINS by abundance: (1) ALBUMIN ~60%. (2) GLOBULINS ~36% — α, β, γ types; γ-globulins are antibodies (immunoglobulins). (3) FIBRINOGEN ~4% — clotting factor I. (4) Trace: enzymes, hormones, transferrin, etc. CLINICAL: LOW ALBUMIN (hypoalbuminemia) → liver disease, malnutrition, kidney disease (loss in urine), burns. Symptom: EDEMA (swelling, esp. legs, abdomen). HIGH ALBUMIN: rare, usually dehydration. KEY DISTINCTIONS: HEMOGLOBIN — protein in RED BLOOD CELLS (not plasma). Carries oxygen. INSULIN — small peptide hormone from PANCREAS, not liver. ANTIBODIES (immunoglobulins) — made by B-cell PLASMA cells (immune system), not liver. CONCEPT: liver is the BODY's master PROTEIN FACTORY (except for immunoglobulins). NUTRITIONAL: dietary protein intake → liver makes plasma proteins. PYQ FREQUENCY: plasma proteins in NEET, AIIMS — 1× per paper.

questions.stem: Which vitamin requires BILE for proper absorption?
questions.explanation: FAT-SOLUBLE VITAMINS — A, D, E, K — require BILE for ABSORPTION. Bile salts EMULSIFY DIETARY FATS (and the fat-soluble vitamins dissolved in them) into MICELLES, allowing intestinal absorption. WATER-SOLUBLE VITAMINS — B-COMPLEX (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9, B12) and C — absorbed directly from intestinal cells without bile assistance. MNEMONIC for fat-soluble: 'A.D.E.K.' (or 'A Dam-fine vitamin Kombo'). VITAMIN A: vision (rhodopsin in retina), skin, immunity. Sources: liver, eggs, dairy, beta-carotene in carrots/spinach. Deficiency: night blindness, xerophthalmia. VITAMIN D: calcium absorption, bone health, immunity. Sources: SUN exposure (UVB skin synthesis), fatty fish, fortified milk. Deficiency: rickets (kids), osteomalacia (adults), increased infection risk. INDIA — widespread vitamin D deficiency (despite sunlight!) due to indoor lifestyle. VITAMIN E: antioxidant, cell membrane protection. Sources: nuts, seeds, oils. Rare deficiency. VITAMIN K: blood clotting. Sources: leafy greens, gut bacteria. Newborns get vitamin K injection at birth. STORAGE: fat-soluble vitamins are STORED in LIVER + ADIPOSE TISSUE; OVERDOSE possible (esp. A, D). Water-soluble are eliminated in urine — daily intake needed. PYQ FREQUENCY: vitamin classification in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.
